strings: Euclid
A language for mathematical proof
Working in ancient Alexandria, Euclid organized geometry and number theory into the Elements. Definitions, postulates and deductions became an enduring model of mathematical exposition.
An axiomatic theory distinguishes its assumptions from what follows logically. Euclid's architecture of proof became an intellectual reference point for later geometry and foundations.
What is the simplest example of a language for mathematical proof?
Which assumptions are essential to the signature result?
Which connected idea would you explore next?
MacTutor · historical biography
Archimedes
Measuring the curved world
Archimedes combined geometry, mechanics and ingenious limiting arguments. He found exact areas and volumes and obtained rigorous bounds on π.
His method of exhaustion traps a curved quantity between simpler approximations. This is an important historical predecessor of integral calculus, not calculus in its modern formulation.
What is the simplest example of measuring the curved world?
Diophantus
Equations with arithmetic constraints
Diophantus's Arithmetica studies numerical problems through equations, often seeking rational solutions. His name became attached to equations whose solutions are constrained to integers.
Asking for integer or rational solutions changes an algebraic problem completely. This arithmetic perspective ultimately reaches modern number theory and questions of decidability.
What is the simplest example of equations with arithmetic constraints?
Aryabhata
Algorithms for astronomy and arithmetic
Aryabhata composed the Aryabhatiya, combining astronomy with computational mathematics. It includes methods for numerical calculation, trigonometry and indeterminate equations.
His work illustrates an early algorithmic culture: a mathematical method can be specified as a sequence of reliable computational steps.
What is the simplest example of algorithms for astronomy and arithmetic?
Al-Khwarizmi
Systematic algebra

Al-Khwarizmi worked in the mathematical culture of Abbasid Baghdad. His algebraic treatise systematized the solution of linear and quadratic equations, and his arithmetic writings helped transmit positional calculation.
The words algebra and algorithm reflect the reception of his work. His equations were expressed rhetorically rather than in today's symbolic notation.
What is the simplest example of systematic algebra?
Omar Khayyam
Cubic equations meet geometry
Omar Khayyam was a mathematician, astronomer and poet. He classified cubic equations and treated many of them geometrically through intersections of conic sections.
Curves can encode algebraic relations, and an intersection can represent a solution. His work predates the fully developed coordinate geometry of Descartes.
What is the simplest example of cubic equations meet geometry?
Fibonacci
Arithmetic travels across cultures
Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci, promoted Hindu–Arabic arithmetic in Latin Europe through Liber abaci. Its problems connect practical calculation with number theory.
A simple recurrence produces a rich mathematical sequence. The rabbit problem is only a small part of his much broader contribution to computation and arithmetic.
What is the simplest example of arithmetic travels across cultures?
René Descartes
Geometry in coordinates
Descartes helped develop analytic geometry by translating geometric problems into equations. His work made symbolic algebra a systematic instrument for studying curves.
Coordinates allow geometric questions to become algebraic calculations. This bridge underlies much of calculus, linear algebra and mathematical modeling.
What is the simplest example of geometry in coordinates?
Pierre de Fermat
Arithmetic problems with long afterlives
Fermat contributed to number theory, analytic geometry, optimization and probability. Many of his assertions became starting points for generations of later mathematics.
For prime p, this congruence is a basic tool of modular arithmetic. His work helped turn patterns among integers into a sustained theoretical program.
What is the simplest example of arithmetic problems with long afterlives?
Blaise Pascal
Counting the uncertain
Pascal worked on geometry, calculation and probability. His correspondence with Fermat helped develop mathematical reasoning about games of chance.
Pascal's triangle organizes binomial coefficients. The same recurrence connects counting, probability and algebraic expansion.
What is the simplest example of counting the uncertain?
Isaac Newton
Change becomes calculable
Newton developed calculus and used mathematics to formulate laws of motion and gravitation. His mathematical physics showed how differential equations can describe a changing world.
Rates of change and accumulated quantities became calculable parts of a physical theory. Calculus was developed independently by Leibniz in a different notation.
What is the simplest example of change becomes calculable?
G. W. Leibniz
A calculus of symbols
Leibniz independently developed calculus and advocated systematic symbolic reasoning. His differential and integral notation became particularly influential.

A good symbolic language can make transformations easier to discover and communicate. His wider logical ambitions anticipated later formal approaches without already constituting modern computation theory.
What is the simplest example of a calculus of symbols?
Leonhard Euler
Connections across mathematics
Euler worked across analysis, number theory, geometry, mechanics and combinatorics. His solution of the Königsberg bridge problem is a foundational episode in graph theory.
Euler repeatedly discovered that distinct mathematical languages describe the same structure. His identity links exponential functions, complex numbers and trigonometry.
What is the simplest example of connections across mathematics?
Joseph-Louis Lagrange
Optimization through structure
Lagrange developed analytical mechanics and the calculus of variations. His multiplier method incorporates equality constraints into optimization.
At a regular constrained optimum, the objective cannot change in a feasible tangent direction. This observation becomes a systematic method for solving constrained problems.
What is the simplest example of optimization through structure?
Pierre-Simon Laplace
Probability as a mathematical theory
Laplace made major contributions to celestial mechanics, probability and analysis. He systematized probabilistic methods for inference and approximation.
The Laplace equation links equilibrium, potential theory and geometry. His probability work helped make uncertainty a subject of rigorous quantitative analysis.
What is the simplest example of probability as a mathematical theory?
Joseph Fourier
Decompose a signal into frequencies
Fourier studied heat flow using expansions into trigonometric components. Fourier analysis became a central way of understanding functions and differential equations.
A complicated function can be studied through simpler oscillations. The conditions and meaning of convergence matter, and became major questions in analysis.
What is the simplest example of decompose a signal into frequencies?
Carl Friedrich Gauss
Arithmetic, geometry and precision
Gauss shaped number theory, geometry, statistics and mathematical astronomy. Disquisitiones Arithmeticae placed congruences and quadratic forms at the center of arithmetic.
Modular arithmetic isolates the structure of remainders. Gauss's work gave later number theory both foundational results and a standard of conceptual precision.
What is the simplest example of arithmetic, geometry and precision?
Augustin-Louis Cauchy
Rigorous analysis
Cauchy helped reorganize analysis around precise concepts of convergence and continuity. He also developed central parts of complex analysis.
Under the Cauchy integral formula's hypotheses, values inside a contour are determined by boundary data. Holomorphic functions consequently have extraordinary rigidity.
What is the simplest example of rigorous analysis?
Évariste Galois
Symmetry explains solvability
Galois related polynomial equations to permutation groups of their roots. His work transformed the question of solving equations by radicals into a structural question about groups.
A polynomial's hidden symmetries govern which algebraic operations can recover its roots. The approach made group theory central to algebra.
What is the simplest example of symmetry explains solvability?
George Boole
Logic becomes algebra
Boole introduced an algebraic treatment of logical reasoning. His work helped establish the idea that logical operations can be manipulated symbolically.
Boolean algebra eventually became a foundation of digital circuit design. Shannon supplied the explicit engineering bridge to switching circuits.
What is the simplest example of logic becomes algebra?
Ada Lovelace
Programs before electronic computers

Lovelace's notes on Babbage's Analytical Engine included a detailed scheme for computing Bernoulli numbers. She also considered how a general symbolic machine might manipulate more than numerical quantities.
Her importance lies in the conception and explanation of programmable symbolic machinery. The Analytical Engine itself was not completed in her lifetime.
What is the simplest example of programs before electronic computers?
Arthur Cayley
Algebraic structures in their own right
Cayley developed matrix theory and abstract group theory. He also contributed to invariant theory and the enumeration of combinatorial structures.
Every group acts faithfully on itself by left multiplication. Cayley's theorem makes an abstract group concrete as a group of permutations.
What is the simplest example of algebraic structures in their own right?
Bernhard Riemann
Geometry beyond flat space
Riemann introduced a flexible framework for curved spaces and made profound contributions to complex analysis and number theory. His 1854 geometry lecture changed the meaning of space in mathematics.
A metric can vary from point to point. This permits intrinsic geometry on manifolds and later became essential to general relativity.
What is the simplest example of geometry beyond flat space?
Richard Dedekind
Numbers defined by structure
Dedekind developed structural foundations for the real numbers and algebraic number theory. Ideals provide a replacement for unique factorization of elements in settings where it fails.
A real number can be described through a partition of the rationals. Structural definitions clarify what an object is without depending on a particular numerical approximation.
What is the simplest example of numbers defined by structure?
Georg Cantor
Different sizes of infinity
Cantor founded set theory and distinguished countable from uncountable infinity. His diagonal argument demonstrates limits on attempts to enumerate all infinite binary sequences.
Infinity is not one undifferentiated size. Diagonalization also became a recurring tool in logic and computability.
What is the simplest example of different sizes of infinity?
Gottlob Frege
Quantifiers and formal reasoning
Frege developed a powerful formal notation for logic in his Begriffsschrift. His work brought quantification and the structure of mathematical inference into a precise symbolic system.
Modern predicate logic owes much to the distinction between objects, functions and quantified assertions. Frege's later foundational system also exposed the dangers of unrestricted comprehension.
What is the simplest example of quantifiers and formal reasoning?
Henri Poincaré
Shape and dynamics
Poincaré helped create algebraic topology and qualitative dynamical systems. He studied global structure rather than relying only on explicit solutions of equations.
The fundamental group records how loops can wind through a space. It translates a geometric problem into an algebraic invariant.
What is the simplest example of shape and dynamics?
Andrey Markov
Randomness with memory of the present
Markov studied stochastic processes whose next state depends on the present state. These processes became a basic model of dependent randomness.
A transition matrix turns long-term random behavior into a problem in probability and linear algebra. Markov chains are central to sampling and randomized algorithms.
What is the simplest example of randomness with memory of the present?
Giuseppe Peano
Arithmetic from axioms
Peano developed an influential axiomatization and notation for arithmetic. He also constructed a continuous space-filling curve, challenging geometric intuition.
A small collection of axioms can support systematic reasoning about numbers. First-order arithmetic nevertheless has nonstandard models and is subject to incompleteness.
What is the simplest example of arithmetic from axioms?
David Hilbert
Certificates, axioms and algebra
Hilbert transformed invariant theory, algebraic geometry and mathematical foundations. His work linked finite generation, algebraic certificates and ambitious programs for formal proof.
Over an algebraically closed field, a finite polynomial system with no common zero admits this Nullstellensatz certificate. Existence of a certificate does not guarantee that it is small.
How does a CNF clause become a polynomial equation?
What is the difference between certificate degree and size?
Why does finite generation not imply efficient decidability?
Bertrand Russell
A paradox at the foundations
Russell's paradox showed that unrestricted set formation is inconsistent. With Whitehead, he pursued a systematic logical foundation for mathematics in Principia Mathematica.
Asking whether R contains itself gives a contradiction. The lesson is about restrictions on a formal system, not an inconsistency of every theory of sets.
What is the simplest example of a paradox at the foundations?
Henri Lebesgue
A more flexible integral
Lebesgue developed measure and integration that accommodate limits and irregular functions far better than the classical Riemann framework.
Measuring the sizes of level sets offers a powerful way to integrate. The resulting framework supports modern probability and functional analysis.
What is the simplest example of a more flexible integral?
G. H. Hardy
Analysis in the service of numbers
Hardy worked in analysis and analytic number theory, notably with Littlewood and Ramanujan. Their methods brought estimates, asymptotics and complex analysis to arithmetic questions.
The Hardy–Ramanujan asymptotic estimates the number of integer partitions. It exemplifies how analysis can reveal the growth of a discrete counting function.
What is the simplest example of analysis in the service of numbers?
L. E. J. Brouwer
A point that cannot move
Brouwer proved foundational results in topology, including his fixed-point theorem. He also developed intuitionism, a distinct philosophy of mathematical proof.
Every continuous self-map of a closed Euclidean ball has a fixed point. This existence theorem became central to equilibrium theory and computational fixed-point problems.
What is the simplest example of a point that cannot move?
Emmy Noether
Structure and symmetry
Noether reshaped abstract algebra through structural methods and established a fundamental relation between continuous symmetries and conservation laws.
Noether's theorem applies under precise variational hypotheses. Her separate algebraic work made rings, ideals and modules central organizing objects.
What is the simplest example of structure and symmetry?
Srinivasa Ramanujan
Unexpected arithmetic patterns
Ramanujan made extraordinary contributions to partitions, series, continued fractions and modular forms. His collaboration with Hardy connected his discoveries to analytic number theory.
A simple-looking congruence reflects deep structure in generating functions. His notebooks continued to generate mathematical work long after his death.
What is the simplest example of unexpected arithmetic patterns?
Stefan Banach
Infinite-dimensional geometry
Banach helped establish functional analysis as a systematic subject. Complete normed vector spaces allow functions themselves to be treated as geometric points.
A contraction on a complete metric space has a unique fixed point. Repeated iteration converges to it, connecting existence with an explicit method.
What is the simplest example of infinite-dimensional geometry?
Norbert Wiener
Feedback, noise and control
Wiener worked on probability, harmonic analysis and cybernetics. He treated communication and control as systems involving noise, prediction and feedback.
Feedback changes a system in response to its observed behavior. His work connected rigorous stochastic analysis with engineering and the study of adaptive systems.
What is the simplest example of feedback, noise and control?
Emil Post
Computation through rewriting
Post developed formal production systems, work on recursive enumerability, and the Post correspondence problem. His approaches helped map the limits of effective procedures.
The Post correspondence problem asks whether tiles can be matched into equal strings. Its undecidability provides a powerful source problem for reductions.
What is the simplest example of computation through rewriting?
Alfred Tarski
Truth, models and decidability
Tarski gave a mathematical account of truth in formal languages and contributed to model theory and algebraic logic. He established decidability for the first-order theory of real closed fields.
Semantic consequence means truth in every model of the axioms. The connection between syntax and semantics became fundamental to logic.
What is the simplest example of truth, models and decidability?
Andrey Kolmogorov
Probability from axioms
Kolmogorov formulated the measure-theoretic axioms of probability and later developed major ideas in randomness and algorithmic information.
For pairwise disjoint events, countable additivity organizes probability into measure theory. His separate complexity notion measures the length of the shortest effective description.
What is the simplest example of probability from axioms?
Alonzo Church
Functions as computation
Church introduced lambda calculus and proved an undecidability result for first-order logic. Lambda calculus became a foundational model of computation and programming-language semantics.
Computation can be expressed through substitution and function application. Different formal models agreeing on computability helped motivate the Church–Turing thesis.
What is the simplest example of functions as computation?
John von Neumann
Mathematics for machines and games

Von Neumann contributed to game theory, operator algebras, quantum foundations and computing. His EDVAC report was an influential account of stored-program design developed in a broader collaborative setting.
The minimax theorem gives finite two-player zero-sum games a common value when mixed strategies are allowed. It connects strategic choice with convex optimization.
Why does randomization make minimax true?
How does a zero-sum game become a linear program?
What is the mathematical role of an operator algebra?
Kurt Gödel
The limits of formal proof
Gödel proved the completeness theorem for first-order logic and the incompleteness theorems for effective arithmetic theories. He also developed the constructible universe in set theory.
Logical completeness concerns truth in all models. Arithmetic incompleteness concerns what a particular effectively axiomatized consistent theory can decide.
How does arithmetic encode a proof?
Why do nonstandard models reconcile completeness and incompleteness?
How do Gödel’s and Turing’s diagonal arguments differ?
Grace Hopper
From machine instructions to languages
Hopper worked on early computers, automatic programming and compiler development. She played an important role in the movement toward machine-independent business programming languages.
Higher-level languages separate what a program expresses from one machine's instruction set. This made programming accessible at a much larger scale.
What is the simplest example of from machine instructions to languages?
Hassler Whitney
Independence beyond vectors
Whitney introduced matroids as a way to axiomatize independence, while also making foundational contributions to differential topology.
The exchange axiom unifies linear independence with forests in graphs. This abstraction later became central to combinatorial optimization.
What is the simplest example of independence beyond vectors?
Stephen Kleene
The structure of effective computation
Kleene developed recursive function theory and major parts of mathematical logic. His work on regular events also helped establish the theory behind regular expressions.
Kleene star expresses arbitrary finite repetition. The equivalence of regular expressions and finite automata connects symbolic pattern descriptions with machines.
What is the simplest example of the structure of effective computation?
Stanislaw Ulam
Random sampling as a method
Ulam made contributions to set theory, analysis and combinatorics. With collaborators he helped develop Monte Carlo methods for numerical problems.
Sampling can estimate a quantity that is difficult to compute exactly. The error depends on the distribution, variance and sampling method, not merely on the sample count.
What is the simplest example of random sampling as a method?
Alan Turing
A mathematical model of computation
Turing defined an abstract computing machine, established universal simulation and proved an undecidability result. His later work included cryptanalysis, machine intelligence and morphogenesis.
One machine can simulate the description of another. Encoding programs as data makes universality and diagonal arguments possible.
How is universal simulation encoded?
How can halting reduce to a concrete combinatorial problem?
Which statements about program behavior are decidable under restrictions?
Paul Erdős
Existence through randomness
Erdős transformed combinatorics through the probabilistic method and developed random graph theory with Rényi. He created influential problems and collaborations across many areas.
For a nonnegative integer-valued X, expectation below one forces an outcome with no counted defects. This turns a probability estimate into an existence proof.
How do you balance short-cycle counts against independence number?
When can conditional expectations derandomize an existence proof?
What changes when maximum degree is fixed in advance?
George Dantzig
Linear optimization at scale
Dantzig developed the simplex method for linear programming. The method and its applications helped establish operations research and computational optimization.
A linear program has geometric structure that can be exploited algorithmically. Simplex is highly influential despite exponential worst-case examples.
What is the simplest example of linear optimization at scale?
Claude Shannon
Information becomes a quantity
Shannon linked Boolean algebra to switching circuits and founded information theory. Entropy, channel capacity and coding theorems made communication limits mathematically precise.
Entropy measures average information under a distribution. For an independent identically distributed source, it controls asymptotic lossless compression rates.
How does typical-set compression work?
Why are zero-error and vanishing-error capacity different?
How can a graph encode confusable symbols?
Herbert Simon
Intelligence as problem solving
Simon studied decision-making, bounded rationality and artificial intelligence. With Allen Newell he built influential models of heuristic problem solving.
A decision-maker may seek a satisfactory solution rather than solve an idealized global optimization problem. This connects cognitive modeling with computational constraints.
What is the simplest example of intelligence as problem solving?
Computer science as empirical inquiry: Symbols and search · Newell and Simon
ACM · Herbert Simon
W. T. Tutte
The structure of matchings and flows
Tutte established foundational results in graph theory, including a characterization of graphs with perfect matchings. His work shaped chromatic and flow theory.
A finite graph has a perfect matching exactly when every deleted vertex set leaves at most that many odd components. The condition reveals global obstructions to pairing.
What is the simplest example of the structure of matchings and flows?
Richard Bellman
Solve once, reuse the answer
Bellman developed dynamic programming: organize a problem into overlapping subproblems whose optimal values satisfy a recurrence.
The displayed Bellman equation is a discounted decision-process form. The broader principle of optimality became central to optimization, control and algorithm design.
What is the simplest example of solve once, reuse the answer?
Edgar F. Codd
Data as relations
Codd proposed the relational model for databases. He separated logical data organization from low-level storage details.
Selection, projection and join describe data manipulation algebraically. The relational viewpoint reshaped database design and query languages.
What is the simplest example of data as relations?
Relational database: A practical foundation for productivity · Codd
ACM · Edgar F. Codd
John Backus
High-level programming
Backus led the team that developed FORTRAN and helped shape programming-language notation. He later advocated function-level programming.
An effective high-level language can express scientific computation while allowing compilation to efficient machine code. Language design itself became a serious theoretical discipline.
What is the simplest example of high-level programming?
Can programming be liberated from the von Neumann style? · Backus
ACM · John Backus
Jean-Pierre Serre
Topology meets algebraic geometry
Serre made foundational contributions to topology, algebraic geometry and number theory. His work brought powerful algebraic methods into the study of spaces.
Cohomology records global information from local algebraic data. Serre's work helped build bridges among formerly distinct mathematical subjects.
What is the simplest example of topology meets algebraic geometry?
John McCarthy
A language for symbolic intelligence
McCarthy helped establish artificial intelligence as a field and designed Lisp. He also worked on formalizing common-sense reasoning.
Symbolic data and programs can be represented in closely related forms. Lisp made recursive symbolic computation an influential programming style.
What is the simplest example of a language for symbolic intelligence?
John McCarthy · Stanford research archive
Marvin Minsky
Models of intelligence
Minsky helped shape early artificial intelligence through work on learning, representation and computation. With Papert, he studied the expressive limitations of perceptrons.
A computational theory of intelligence must explain both representation and procedure. His work influenced symbolic AI and debates about learning architectures.
What is the simplest example of models of intelligence?
ACM · Marvin Minsky
Allen Newell
Heuristic search for reasoning
Newell, with Simon and collaborators, developed early programs for logical problem solving. He later worked on unified theories of cognition.
Problem solving can be organized as search through states. Heuristics guide the search without changing the distinction between finding a proof and checking it.
What is the simplest example of heuristic search for reasoning?
ACM · Allen Newell
John Nash
Equilibrium beyond zero-sum games
Nash proved the existence of mixed-strategy equilibria in finite games. He also made major contributions to geometry and partial differential equations.
No player can gain through a unilateral deviation. Equilibrium need not be unique, efficient or reached by a natural learning process.
How does the fixed-point map encode best responses?
What precisely makes END OF LINE a total search problem?
Why can a three-player equilibrium require irrational numbers?
Alexander Grothendieck
A new language for geometry
Grothendieck rebuilt major parts of algebraic geometry around schemes, functors and cohomology. His methods allow geometric reasoning over rings as well as fields.
A scheme retains information, including infinitesimal structure, that an ordinary set of solutions may lose. This framework transformed arithmetic geometry.
Why does a nilpotent element carry geometric information?
What does changing the base from Z to Fₚ do?
What do orbit closures mean in algebraic complexity?
Michael Atiyah
Analysis detects topology
Atiyah helped develop topological K-theory and, with Isadore Singer, proved the index theorem. The result connects differential operators with topological data.
An analytic count involving the kernel and cokernel of an elliptic operator can be computed from geometric-topological invariants.
What is the simplest example of analysis detects topology?
Edsger Dijkstra
Algorithms with invariants
Dijkstra developed influential algorithms and methods for structured programming and correctness. His shortest-path algorithm is a model of greedy reasoning.
With nonnegative edge weights, the closest unsettled vertex can be finalized safely. The proof invariant is as important as the implementation.
What is the simplest example of algorithms with invariants?
Michael Rabin
Randomness as an algorithmic resource
Rabin contributed to automata theory, logic, randomized algorithms and cryptography. His primality test made probabilistic computation a practical mathematical tool.
An algorithm can have a rigorous error guarantee without being deterministic. The distribution and independence assumptions are part of the guarantee.
What is the simplest example of randomness as an algorithmic resource?
Finite automata and their decision problems · Rabin and Scott
ACM · Michael Rabin
Dana Scott
Meaning for recursive programs
Scott contributed to automata theory, logic and the mathematical semantics of programming languages. Domain theory supplies ordered spaces in which recursive definitions have meanings.
A recursive specification is a fixed-point equation. Suitable ordered structures allow a least solution to be built from increasing approximations.
What is the simplest example of meaning for recursive programs?
Logic and programming languages · Scott
ACM · Dana Scott
C. A. R. Hoare
Programs as mathematical claims
Hoare introduced a logic for program correctness and developed influential algorithms, including quicksort. His logic separates preconditions, execution and postconditions.
A Hoare triple expresses that, when C terminates from a state satisfying P, the resulting state satisfies Q. Termination requires additional reasoning for total correctness.
What is the simplest example of programs as mathematical claims?
ACM · C. A. R. Hoare
Jack Edmonds
Efficient combinatorial optimization
Edmonds developed polynomial-time matching algorithms and polyhedral descriptions of combinatorial problems. His work helped clarify efficient computation as a mathematical objective.
Odd cycles obstruct the simple bipartite augmenting-path method. Contracting a blossom preserves the essential search problem and makes a general algorithm possible.
What is the simplest example of efficient combinatorial optimization?
INFORMS · Jack Edmonds
Robin Milner
Types, proofs and communication
Milner contributed to automated reasoning, programming-language design and concurrency theory. His work includes LCF, ML and process calculi.
Concurrent processes interact rather than execute as one sequential thread. His formalisms let researchers reason systematically about communication and behavior.
What is the simplest example of types, proofs and communication?
Elements of interaction · Milner
ACM · Robin Milner
Richard Karp
A network of hard problems
Karp's 1972 paper established NP-completeness for 21 natural combinatorial problems. He also made major contributions to algorithms and randomization.
A polynomial-time reduction transfers an efficient algorithm for B into one for A. Starting with Cook–Levin, reductions made hardness reusable across mathematical domains.
Can you verify both directions of the clique reduction?
What must an approximation-preserving reduction preserve?
How does a randomized fingerprint avoid reading two objects repeatedly?
ACM · Richard Karp and computational complexity
Robert Floyd
Proving programs correct
Floyd developed foundational approaches to program verification and influential algorithms. His work ties assertions about program states to control flow.
An invariant explains what remains true through a computation. A separate progress argument is needed to establish termination.
What is the simplest example of proving programs correct?
The paradigms of programming · Floyd
ACM · Robert Floyd
Judea Pearl
From association to intervention
Pearl developed influential methods for probabilistic reasoning and causal inference. Bayesian networks and structural causal models express different kinds of dependence.
An intervention changes the mechanism generating X rather than merely conditioning on its observed value. Causal conclusions require assumptions encoded in the model.
What is the simplest example of from association to intervention?
Causality · author’s research page
Donald Knuth
The analysis of algorithms
Knuth systematized algorithmic knowledge in The Art of Computer Programming. He also created TeX and developed literate programming.
Correctness does not settle efficiency. Knuth's work combines implementation detail, combinatorial analysis and mathematical exposition.
What is the simplest example of the analysis of algorithms?
Stephen Cook
The first universal NP problem
Cook proved that satisfiability can encode every polynomial-time nondeterministic computation. Levin independently developed closely related completeness ideas.
Cook–Levin establishes a starting point for NP-completeness. The theorem does not prove that SAT requires superpolynomial time.
What is the simplest example of the first universal np problem?
ACM · Stephen Cook and NP-completeness
John Hopcroft
Efficient structure in algorithms
Hopcroft contributed to automata theory and the design and analysis of algorithms. His work with Karp and Tarjan produced fundamental graph algorithms.
The Hopcroft–Karp bound for bipartite matching comes from augmenting many shortest paths in phases. A structural argument controls the number of phases.
What is the simplest example of efficient structure in algorithms?
ACM · John Hopcroft
Endre Szemerédi
Order inside dense sets
Szemerédi proved that every positive-density set of integers contains arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions. He also introduced the graph regularity lemma.
Density can force organized patterns without periodicity. His results reshaped extremal combinatorics and connected it with ergodic and additive methods.
What is the simplest example of order inside dense sets?
Pierre Deligne
The Weil conjectures
Deligne proved the remaining Riemann-hypothesis part of the Weil conjectures using the cohomological framework developed by Grothendieck and others.
Frobenius eigenvalues on the relevant cohomology have prescribed magnitudes. This links point counts over finite fields with deep geometric structure.
What is the simplest example of the weil conjectures?
Whitfield Diffie
Secrets over a public channel
Diffie and Hellman's work established public-key cryptography as a major paradigm. Key exchange allows parties to derive a shared secret using public messages.
The shared algebraic value is easy for participants to obtain but should be hard for an observer to recover under the chosen group's computational assumptions.
What is the simplest example of secrets over a public channel?
New directions in cryptography · Diffie and Hellman
Martin Hellman
Public-key cryptography
Hellman, with Diffie and other contributors, helped establish modern public-key cryptography. The work changed assumptions about secure communication and prior shared secrets.
The algebraic identity alone is not security. Parameter choices, protocols and computational assumptions determine whether an implementation is secure.
What is the simplest example of public-key cryptography?
ACM · Martin Hellman
Leonard Adleman
Computation across representations
Adleman co-developed RSA with Rivest and Shamir. He later demonstrated a molecular computation using DNA to solve a small combinatorial instance.
RSA uses a trapdoor-style arithmetic structure; secure encryption additionally requires an appropriate encoding protocol. Adleman's DNA work explored a very different computational substrate.
What is the simplest example of computation across representations?
ACM · Leonard Adleman
Andrew Yao
Randomness, communication and security
Yao developed fundamental ideas in randomized algorithms, communication complexity and cryptography. His minimax principle is a central lower-bound tool.
Under the relevant finite minimax formulation, a hard input distribution can lower-bound randomized algorithms. This changes a randomized lower bound into a distributional problem.
What is the simplest example of randomness, communication and security?
ACM · Andrew Yao
William Thurston
Three-dimensional geometry
Thurston transformed low-dimensional topology through hyperbolic geometry and the geometrization program. He showed how geometry can organize the classification of three-manifolds.
A complicated manifold can be studied through canonical pieces carrying geometric structures. Perelman's later work completed geometrization via Ricci flow.
What is the simplest example of three-dimensional geometry?
Alain Connes
Geometry without commuting coordinates
Connes developed noncommutative geometry and major parts of operator-algebra theory. Algebraic structures become geometric objects even when multiplication is noncommutative.
Replacing functions on a space by a noncommutative algebra extends geometric reasoning to new settings. The connection also reaches mathematical physics and quantum theory.
What is the simplest example of geometry without commuting coordinates?
Ron Rivest
Public-key algorithms
Rivest co-developed RSA and contributed broadly to algorithms and cryptography. His work connects computational difficulty with practical constructions.
A public transformation can be easy to apply while reversal requires secret information or a hard computation. Bare algebraic RSA is not a complete secure encryption protocol.
What is the simplest example of public-key algorithms?
ACM · Ron Rivest
Leonid Levin
Universal search and completeness
Levin independently established foundational completeness results and developed algorithmic information theory and average-case complexity.
Worst-case difficulty and typical-instance difficulty are different. Levin's frameworks make the input distribution and verification process part of the mathematical problem.
What is the simplest example of universal search and completeness?
Leonid Levin · selected research and exposition
Robert Tarjan
Data structures with provable efficiency
Tarjan developed fundamental graph algorithms and data-structure analyses, often with collaborators. Amortized analysis measures the cost of a sequence rather than one isolated operation.
A single expensive step need not make a data structure inefficient. Structural accounting can show that expensive operations cannot occur too often.
What is the simplest example of data structures with provable efficiency?
ACM · Robert Tarjan
László Lovász
Discrete questions, richer spaces
Lovász connected combinatorics with probability, topology, optimization and graph limits. His local lemma, theta function and topological methods became major tools.
The theta function bridges an intractable combinatorial quantity and semidefinite optimization. It also gives a multiplicative upper bound for Shannon capacity.
Why is pairwise independence not enough for the Local Lemma?
Can you derive the theta SDP from an independent set?
What information does a graphon retain that a local graph limit does not?
Leslie Valiant
Counting, circuits and learning
Valiant introduced counting complexity, developed algebraic complexity and formulated PAC learning. He showed that changing the information requested can change a problem's complexity.
For a zero–one bipartite adjacency matrix, the permanent counts perfect matchings. Computing it is #P-complete under polynomial-time counting reductions.

Encode the same message with A = 0, B = 10, C = 110, D = 111. Count the bits and decode your result from left to right.
Explain why no codeword is the beginning of another. Try DDDD and compare the lengths again; account for the codebook separately if you would transmit it.
Two encoded messages and an example showing when the variable-length code helps.
A tempting choice goes wrong
Test a greedy rule for the 0–1 knapsack problem: each item is indivisible.
Set capacity to 50. Use three items with (weight, value) equal to (10, 60), (20, 100), and (30, 120). Calculate each value-to-weight ratio.
Take items in decreasing ratio order whenever they fit. Record the final weight and value.
List all eight subsets, discard those over capacity, and find the best remaining value. State exactly which greedy rule your example disproves.
A complete small counterexample, including the greedy and optimal choices.
One edge changes everything
Find the edges that hold a network together.
Draw two disjoint four-cycles. Join one vertex of the first to one vertex of the second with a single edge.
For every edge, imagine deleting it while keeping all vertices. Mark it as a bridge precisely when the graph becomes disconnected.
Add a second edge between a different pair of vertices across the two cycles. Repeat the deletion test and explain what happened to the original bridge.
Two annotated graphs and an explanation using an alternative path.
Find a route one choice at a time
Run Dijkstra’s algorithm by hand on a small undirected weighted graph.
Draw vertices A through F and edges AB:4, AC:1, CB:2, BD:1, CD:5, DE:3, CF:7, and FE:1. Start from A.

Set A’s tentative distance to zero and all others to infinity. Repeatedly settle the unsettled vertex with the smallest distance. For each unsettled neighbor, keep the smaller of its old distance and the settled distance plus the connecting edge’s weight.
Record which predecessor gave each improvement and reconstruct one shortest path from A to E. Consider how a later negative edge could undermine a distance you already settled.
A distance table, a shortest path, and one sentence explaining the crucial assumption.
Draw an idea before naming it
Make a small abstract drawing about connection.
Choose five points on a page. Connect some pairs with red curves and some pairs with blue curves. Keep a small record of which pairs are connected.
Redraw the same connections with the points in different positions. Let the new drawing have a different mood.
Give each drawing a title. Write one sentence describing what changed visually and one describing what stayed the same mathematically.
Two drawings of the same colored graph with different visual personalities.
A question in three quiet shots
Plan a tiny film about noticing something you usually pass by.
Choose an ordinary object or place within reach: a window, an empty chair, a cup, or a doorway. Write one question it suggests.
Sketch three shots: the setting, one revealing detail, and the setting again. Give each a duration and one sound; no dialogue is needed.
Record the shots with your phone or keep the storyboard. Describe how the final shot changes what the first shot meant.
A three-frame storyboard or a very short film with one clear question.
Hear two clocks meet
Make a rhythm from two simple repeating rules.
Write beats 1 through 12. Put a red mark on beats divisible by 3 and a blue mark on beats divisible by 4.
Tap a different surface for each color, or draw a score. Move slowly through the twelve beats, combining the taps when both marks appear.
Repeat with periods 3 and 5 across fifteen beats. Predict the next shared beat for each pattern and connect your prediction to the least common multiple.
Two short rhythm scores and a rule for when their accents meet.
